draft.title: Traditional knowledge in conservation
card: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have cared for Country for tens of thousands of years. Traditional knowledge is passed down through generations and includes how species, seasons and land are connected.
Indigenous ranger programs employ people on their own Country. Rangers combine traditional knowledge with tools such as surveys and monitoring, and they work to manage Country.
Rangers can monitor threatened species, and they can control weeds and feral animals that harm native species.
Cultural burning uses planned, low-intensity fires set at suitable times and places. It can reduce fuel for large bushfires and help some plants and habitats.
draft.remember: Traditional knowledge and ranger programs can help manage Country, monitor species and control fire and pests.

a.q: Which activity is an example of an Indigenous ranger program using traditional knowledge in conservation?
opts: Cultural burning on Country to reduce fuel and renew habitat
Fencing off Country to keep all people and fire out
Leaving Country alone so that no fire ever reaches it
Hiring outside crews to set large fires in hot weather
a.why: Cultural burning uses planned, low-intensity fire guided by knowledge of Country, which can reduce fuel and help habitats. Keeping all fire out is wrong because fire is one of the tools rangers use to manage Country.
a.clue: Think about what rangers do with fire on their own Country.

b.q: A ranger group in northern Australia works with Elders to track a threatened mammal and to remove feral animals from its habitat. Why is this approach useful for conservation?
opts: It joins long-held knowledge of Country with field monitoring
It replaces the need for any monitoring of the species
It works only if the group is outside the local community
It protects the mammal by stopping all fire on Country
b.why: Elders hold knowledge of species and places, and rangers can add monitoring and pest control on the ground. This is why the approach helps. It does not replace monitoring, because monitoring is one of the ranger tasks.
b.clue: Look at what the Elders and the rangers each bring.

proposal.title: Traditional knowledge in conservation
card: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have cared for Country for tens of thousands of years. Traditional knowledge, passed down through generations, explains how species, seasons, fire and land are connected.

Indigenous ranger programs employ people to care for their own Country. Rangers combine traditional knowledge with scientific tools such as surveys, camera traps and mapping, so each adds what the other lacks.
Rangers can monitor threatened species where they live, and they can control weeds and feral animals, such as cats and buffalo, that harm native species.

Cultural burning is a traditional practice guided by knowledge of Country, and rangers carry it out. They set small, cool fires at cooler times, such as the early dry season in the north. This can reduce fuel before hotter, later fires and keep a patchwork of habitats.
proposal.remember: Traditional knowledge and scientific tools work together to care for Country, species, fire and pests.

a.q: Why do rangers in northern Australia carry out cultural burning early in the dry season?
opts: Cooler fires then reduce fuel before hotter, later fires
Fuel is driest then, so fires burn hotter and clear more
Burning then clears land for cattle grazing and crops
Smoke then drives feral animals away from native species
a.why: Early in the dry season, fires burn small and cool, which can reduce fuel before the hotter fires later in the year. The idea that fuel is driest then is the reverse: fuel dries out as the season goes on, and cultural burning aims for cool fires, not hot ones.
a.clue: Think about what the fire is meant to prevent later in the year.

b.q: Rangers in the Kimberley search for a threatened bilby. Elders know where its tracks appear after rain, so rangers set camera traps there. Why does this help?
opts: Traditional knowledge guides where survey tools are placed
Elders' knowledge stands in for surveys and camera traps
Rangers from elsewhere add science the community lacks
It moves the bilby off Country into a fenced reserve
b.why: The Elders' knowledge shows where to look, and the camera traps record what is there, so the two work together. The idea that Elders' knowledge stands in for the surveys is wrong, because the rangers still use the camera traps: each kind of knowledge adds to the other.
b.clue: Look at what the Elders and the camera traps each provide.
